name: Dapsone gel (Aczone)
lead: Dapsone gel, sold as Aczone, is a prescription topical gel for acne vulgaris. It is applied to the skin to reduce the red, inflamed pimples and papules that make acne look angry, and it is often used by people who want clearer skin when first-line topicals such as retinoids and benzoyl peroxide have not been enough or are not well tolerated [12]. Wikipedia reports that QLT USA developed the 5% gel in the early 2000s and that the FDA approved a 7.5% gel in February 2016 [1].

Dapsone has both antibacterial and anti-inflammatory actions. Because the skin absorbs little of it, systemic exposure from the gel is far lower than from oral dapsone, which an Aczone review put at 126-fold lower in a phase 1 study; the same review reports that the gel was applied safely in people with G6PD deficiency without causing anemia [11]. Wikipedia likewise reports that the 5% gel did not cause clinically significant hemoglobin declines in people with G6PD deficiency [1].

Many registered trials have studied the gel, including two phase 3 studies enrolling over 2,000 patients each [2][3]. A 2022 systematic review of 14 studies found success rates of 40.1 to 69.4 percent for the 5% gel and 29.8 to 47.0 percent for the 7.5% gel over 12 to 16 weeks, with inflammatory lesions falling by a larger percentage than non-inflammatory ones [12].

paras: The gel treats acne vulgaris. Registered trials covered children aged 9 to 11 [4], women with skin of color [5], truncal acne [6], and maintenance after oral doxycycline [7]. A terminated trial tested 5% gel in dermatitis herpetiformis [8].

Mild irritation, redness, dryness, burning and itching can occur. Use with benzoyl peroxide can cause temporary yellow or orange skin discoloration. Methemoglobinemia is linked in the source to long-term oral dapsone, not the topical gel [1].

As an antibacterial, dapsone inhibits bacterial folate synthesis; as an anti-inflammatory, it inhibits myeloperoxidase [1]. Because it is poorly soluble in water, early topical formulations were hard to develop [1].

The 2022 systematic review of 14 clinical trials reported treatment success ranges of 40.1 to 69.4 percent (5% gel) and 29.8 to 47.0 percent (7.5% gel) after 12 to 16 weeks, with mild irritation in 2.0 to 75.0 percent of participants and no major treatment-related adverse effects, and noted varied regimens across studies as a limitation [12]. A 2022 meta-analysis of randomized trials covering 11,424 participants in 7 trials found dapsone gel, alone or combined with isotretinoin, superior to vehicle; the authors note that, due to side-effect concerns, its clinical application has not been promoted widely [13]. The two identically designed large vehicle-controlled trials of the 7.5% once-daily gel in adolescents and adults were published in 2016 [14].

Other studies: an open-label study in people with skin of color [18], a phase 4 study of 7.5% gel in girls and boys aged 9 to 11 [4], a randomized trial in healthy volunteers comparing the facial irritation of four acne regimens including Aczone 5%, which found no significant overall difference in blinded erythema grading [17], and trials in papulopustular rosacea comparing 5% gel with metronidazole and testing the 7.5% gel [15][16].

sections.h: Use in appearance and skin-care communities
paras: Dapsone gel appears in dermatology reviews as an option for adult women with acne, alongside hormonal therapy, in a 2016 review of new acne and rosacea options [19]. It is positioned as a gentler alternative when retinoids or benzoyl peroxide cause dryness or stinging, though the head-to-head irritation study cited above found the tested regimens generally well tolerated in healthy skin [17].

Two phase 3 trials of dapsone gel in acne enrolled 2,238 and 2,102 patients [2][3]. A phase 1 study compared a test product with Aczone 5% and placebo (n=1134) [9]. A phase 4 trial compared 7.5% gel with 20% trichloroacetic acid [10]. Detailed results are not summarised here.
Dapsone was first synthesised in 1908, studied as an antibiotic in 1937 and used for leprosy from 1945 [1].

timeline.event: Dapsone first studied as an antibiotic [1].

card.summary: Rx anti-inflammatory gel for acne with large phase 3 trial programs; usually mild irritation.
card.note: Can discolor skin when used with benzoyl peroxide.

quick.overview:
Dapsone gel (Aczone) is a prescription topical for acne. It has been studied in large registered trials, including in children and people with skin of color.

It is available in 5% and 7.5% strengths.
quick.mechanism: Dapsone inhibits bacterial folate synthesis and has anti-inflammatory activity through myeloperoxidase inhibition.
quick.risks: Mild irritation, dryness, redness; temporary yellow-orange discoloration with benzoyl peroxide. Prescription-only.

chain: Antibacterial and anti-inflammatory action in the follicle
angle.text: The gel is a prescribed topical for inflammatory acne. Trials show it reduces inflamed lesions more than blackheads and whiteheads, and it is often chosen for skin that is easily irritated.
